I’ve also been told many times that they need a lot of mental and physical energy to even start sewing, let alone complete a project. I get that. But to my brain, the sewing machine goes brrrr and requires no thoughts at all lol.
So the following list is limited by my range of interests and abilities alone. And if it doesn’t sound appealing to you, you’ll just have to sit down one evening with a piece of paper and think about what hobbies you have, used to have, or would like to pick up, and which of them could be done from the comfort of your couch or bed. Basically, anything you can do sitting or lying down will do! Hopefully, you might get some ideas from mine tho ❤

So, in no particular order:
Painting.
An adult coloring book.
Playing with my cat.
Those books where you connect the dots to reveal an image. Not sure what they’re called.
Embroidery, which I do a lot of. The trick is to have a small case with all your supplies ready, so when you want to do some embroidery, it’s easy to pick up. Sashiko can be an interesting one to start with, if any of that sounds exciting to you.
Knitting.
Sewing, but with a caveat, since it depends greatly on the project and the exact stage you’re at.
Jigsaw puzzles.
Beadwork, like making a bracelet or doing beaded embroidery, which I’ve done before.
Doing a tarot spread for myself.
Bedazzling something. Anything, really.
Mending something, like sewing a button back on.
Exploring the night sky through an app where you can tap on visible stars and get information about them. My favorite thing is when I can locate the ISS. I’m not naming any specific apps because a quick search in whichever app store you use will give you plenty of options, and they’re all pretty similar.
Aromatherapy.
Doing my makeup just for the fun of it. It felt bizarre at first to do a full beat with nowhere to go, but now I experiment a lot, try new products, or just cover my face in glitter, which does wonders for my mood, to be honest.
Doodling.
Putting on an album on CD or vinyl and listening to it from start to finish without doing anything else. Just really listening to the music and lyrics and thinking about the artist’s vision and intention.
Making small pottery projects with air-dry clay.
Painting those projects afterwards.
Making small epoxy projects.
Drawing on a tablet if my monkey brain really wants to sit in front of a screen.
I’ve also been trying to digitize my house in software that recreates 2D floor plans in 3D form, and that’s been a huge hit with my monkey brain.
And then again, when I really want to stare at a screen, I’ve been digitizing my closet. It’s become a great substitute for social media because it literally takes hours lol.
Small DIY projects, depending on their size and difficulty.
Small woodworking projects. 
Messing around with my fiancé on his dj deck thingy. 
Doing collages from old magazines. 
Painting something in a glow in the dark paint.
Making candles. 
I’ll add to the list if I think of anything later. 

But I’m curious, what would you add for yourself in a list like this?

The important things with CPTSD is to learn
1) It's not the same as PTSD and the flashbacks are different 
2) to recognise dysregulation, ie "emotional flashbacks", which feel like intense versions of fear or anger, etc.
3) Learning how to identify dysregulation and step back out of situations that are triggering and regulate is essential. You may find yourself getting triggered in conversations without realising it because the trauma isn't necessarily conscious 
4) And to recognise that CBT (which therapists always want to do by default as it's well funded and pushed by the industry) actively _worsens_ CPTSD because of how trauma affects the body and causes dysregulation. You can't just push through dysregulation that way or force yourself to do things like meditation if your body isn't comfortable with it.
Go to a trauma-specialised therapist. Sadly, trauma is a specialisation, not something that all therapists learn how to treat.
5) My experience is that it IS possible to remove triggers. I've been working on my triggers with gentleness and patience and self-regulation and awareness. Many things that used to affect me don't anymore.

Making small epoxy projects.
Drawing on a tablet if my monkey brain really wants to sit in front of a screen.

Small woodworking projects. 
Messing around with my fiancé on his dj deck thingy. 
Doing collages from old magazines. 
Painting something in a glow in the dark paint.
Making candles. 
I’ll add to the list if I think of anything later. 

But I’m curious, what would you add for yourself in a list like this?

Love this! Came here to write the same thing. It’s a nice video but I’d love to add trauma, too much therapy is actually not as good for help for trauma as it should be. And I mean, it’s nearly universal

The important things with CPTSD is to learn
1) It's not the same as PTSD and the flashbacks are different 
2) to recognise dysregulation, ie "emotional flashbacks", which feel like intense versions of fear or anger, etc.
3) Learning how to identify dysregulation and step back out of situations that are triggering and regulate is essential. You may find yourself getting triggered in conversations without realising it because the trauma isn't necessarily conscious 
4) And to recognise that CBT (which therapists always want to do by default as it's well funded and pushed by the industry) actively _worsens_ CPTSD because of how trauma affects the body and causes dysregulation. You can't just push through dysregulation that way or force yourself to do things like meditation if your body isn't comfortable with it.
Go to a trauma-specialised therapist. Sadly, trauma is a specialisation, not something that all therapists learn how to treat.
5) My experience is that it IS possible to remove triggers. I've been working on my triggers with gentleness and patience and self-regulation and awareness. Many things that used to affect me don't anymore.

@tequilabumbum4373 Hi love, sorry for the long wait, I’ve only just seen your comment.
PS: I’ve just typed all of this out, so I thought I’d preface it by saying that I’m into sewing as a whole and DIYs, but that’s not everyone’s cup of tea and that’s okay. And depending on the person, an activity may be interpreted as passive or active due to their interests and abilities.
I’ve mentioned to my friends that sewing is meditative for me and gotten shocked looks in return. I’ve also been told many times that they need a lot of mental and physical energy to even start sewing, let alone complete a project. I get that. But to my brain, the sewing machine goes brrrr and requires no thoughts at all lol.
So the following list is limited by my range of interests and abilities alone. And if it doesn’t sound appealing to you, you’ll just have to sit down one evening with a piece of paper and think about what hobbies you have, used to have, or would like to pick up, and which of them could be done from the comfort of your couch or bed. Basically, anything you can do sitting or lying down will do! Hopefully, you might get some ideas from mine tho ❤

So, in no particular order:
Painting.
An adult coloring book.
Playing with my cat.
Those books where you connect the dots to reveal an image. Not sure what they’re called.
Embroidery, which I do a lot of. The trick is to have a small case with all your supplies ready, so when you want to do some embroidery, it’s easy to pick up. Sashiko can be an interesting one to start with, if any of that sounds exciting to you.
Knitting.
Sewing, but with a caveat, since it depends greatly on the project and the exact stage you’re at.
Jigsaw puzzles.
Beadwork, like making a bracelet or doing beaded embroidery, which I’ve done before.
Doing a tarot spread for myself.
Bedazzling something. Anything, really.
Mending something, like sewing a button back on.
Exploring the night sky through an app where you can tap on visible stars and get information about them. My favorite thing is when I can locate the ISS. I’m not naming any specific apps because a quick search in whichever app store you use will give you plenty of options, and they’re all pretty similar.
Aromatherapy.
Doing my makeup just for the fun of it. It felt bizarre at first to do a full beat with nowhere to go, but now I experiment a lot, try new products, or just cover my face in glitter, which does wonders for my mood, to be honest.
Doodling.
Putting on an album on CD or vinyl and listening to it from start to finish without doing anything else. Just really listening to the music and lyrics and thinking about the artist’s vision and intention.
Making small pottery projects with air-dry clay.
Painting those projects afterwards.
Making small epoxy projects.
Drawing on a tablet if my monkey brain really wants to sit in front of a screen.
I’ve also been trying to digitize my house in software that recreates 2D floor plans in 3D form, and that’s been a huge hit with my monkey brain.
And then again, when I really want to stare at a screen, I’ve been digitizing my closet. It’s become a great substitute for social media because it literally takes hours lol.
Small DIY projects, depending on their size and difficulty.
Small woodworking projects. 
Messing around with my fiancé on his dj deck thingy. 
Doing collages from old magazines. 
Painting something in a glow in the dark paint.
Making candles. 
I’ll add to the list if I think of anything later. 

But I’m curious, what would you add for yourself in a list like this?

The important things with CPTSD is to learn
1) It's not the same as PTSD and the flashbacks are different 
2) to recognise dysregulation, ie "emotional flashbacks", which feel like intense versions of fear or anger, etc.
3) Learning how to identify dysregulation and step back out of situations that are triggering and regulate is essential. You may find yourself getting triggered in conversations without realising it because the trauma isn't necessarily conscious 
4) And to recognise that CBT (which therapists always want to do by default as it's well funded and pushed by the industry) actively _worsens_ CPTSD because of how trauma affects the body and causes dysregulation. You can't just push through dysregulation that way or force yourself to do things like meditation if your body isn't comfortable with it.
Go to a trauma-specialised therapist. Sadly, trauma is a specialisation, not something that all therapists learn how to treat.
5) My experience is that it IS possible to remove triggers. I've been working on my triggers with gentleness and patience and self-regulation and awareness. Many things that used to affect me don't anymore.

When I hear that I'm not broken (after doing a couple years of therapy) the way I interpret their meaning is that my brain and body are responding in exactly the way you would expect under the circumstances. 
The circumstances are a combination of lots of factors like environment, personality, family situation, beliefs, values, etc etc etc but most importantly to me, learned tools. I go to therapy to learn tools to fix my life. It's not me that's broken. I'm just hammering screws. I need better tools and instructions and practice so I can use them right and apply them to my situation and life.
Your life may need fixing, and you will need to work and change. It's not the deep down real you that's broken, though. Just the surroundings.

I’ve mentioned to my friends that sewing is meditative for me and gotten shocked looks in return. I’ve also been told many times that they need a lot of mental and physical energy to even start sewing, let alone complete a project. I get that. But to my brain, the sewing machine goes brrrr and requires no thoughts at all lol.
So the following list is limited by my range of interests and abilities alone. And if it doesn’t sound appealing to you, you’ll just have to sit down one evening with a piece of paper and think about what hobbies you have, used to have, or would like to pick up, and which of them could be done from the comfort of your couch or bed. Basically, anything you can do sitting or lying down will do! Hopefully, you might get some ideas from mine tho ❤

So, in no particular order:
Painting.
An adult coloring book.
Playing with my cat.
Those books where you connect the dots to reveal an image. Not sure what they’re called.
Embroidery, which I do a lot of. The trick is to have a small case with all your supplies ready, so when you want to do some embroidery, it’s easy to pick up. Sashiko can be an interesting one to start with, if any of that sounds exciting to you.
Knitting.
Sewing, but with a caveat, since it depends greatly on the project and the exact stage you’re at.
Jigsaw puzzles.
Beadwork, like making a bracelet or doing beaded embroidery, which I’ve done before.
Doing a tarot spread for myself.
Bedazzling something. Anything, really.
Mending something, like sewing a button back on.
Exploring the night sky through an app where you can tap on visible stars and get information about them. My favorite thing is when I can locate the ISS. I’m not naming any specific apps because a quick search in whichever app store you use will give you plenty of options, and they’re all pretty similar.
Aromatherapy.
Doing my makeup just for the fun of it. It felt bizarre at first to do a full beat with nowhere to go, but now I experiment a lot, try new products, or just cover my face in glitter, which does wonders for my mood, to be honest.
Doodling.
Putting on an album on CD or vinyl and listening to it from start to finish without doing anything else. Just really listening to the music and lyrics and thinking about the artist’s vision and intention.
Making small pottery projects with air-dry clay.
Painting those projects afterwards.
Making small epoxy projects.
Drawing on a tablet if my monkey brain really wants to sit in front of a screen.
I’ve also been trying to digitize my house in software that recreates 2D floor plans in 3D form, and that’s been a huge hit with my monkey brain.
And then again, when I really want to stare at a screen, I’ve been digitizing my closet. It’s become a great substitute for social media because it literally takes hours lol.
Small DIY projects, depending on their size and difficulty.
Small woodworking projects. 
Messing around with my fiancé on his dj deck thingy. 
Doing collages from old magazines. 
Painting something in a glow in the dark paint.
Making candles. 
I’ll add to the list if I think of anything later. 

But I’m curious, what would you add for yourself in a list like this?

The important things with CPTSD is to learn
1) It's not the same as PTSD and the flashbacks are different 
2) to recognise dysregulation, ie "emotional flashbacks", which feel like intense versions of fear or anger, etc.
3) Learning how to identify dysregulation and step back out of situations that are triggering and regulate is essential. You may find yourself getting triggered in conversations without realising it because the trauma isn't necessarily conscious 
4) And to recognise that CBT (which therapists always want to do by default as it's well funded and pushed by the industry) actively _worsens_ CPTSD because of how trauma affects the body and causes dysregulation. You can't just push through dysregulation that way or force yourself to do things like meditation if your body isn't comfortable with it.
Go to a trauma-specialised therapist. Sadly, trauma is a specialisation, not something that all therapists learn how to treat.
5) My experience is that it IS possible to remove triggers. I've been working on my triggers with gentleness and patience and self-regulation and awareness. Many things that used to affect me don't anymore.
